content.tldr: Transport Layer Security (TLS) provides confidentiality, data integrity, and server authentication for Internet traffic through asymmetric key exchange and symmetric cipher streaming.
content.simple_explanation: TLS operates above TCP to secure application layer protocols like HTTPS. In TLS 1.3, the client sends a ClientHello with supported cipher suites and an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key share. The server replies with ServerHello, its key share, and its digital certificate. Both parties derive matching symmetric session keys (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) in a single round-trip (1-RTT), switching to high-throughput symmetric encryption for all application payloads.
content.real_world_example: An armored transport tunnel: before sensitive freight moves, both checkpoints exchange verified credentials and generate a temporary combination lock used exclusively for that specific journey.
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: Supporting obsolete cipher suites like 3DES, RC4, or CBC-mode ciphers leaves servers vulnerable to POODLE, BEAST, or SWEET32 attacks. Production best practices mandate disabling SSL 3.0 through TLS 1.1, enforcing TLS 1.2/1.3, enabling HSTS, and utilizing AEAD ciphers.
